title: Laser microscopy acquisition and analysis of premotor synapses in the murine spinal cord
protocol: Inject 200 mg/kg Metamizole intraperitoneally 30 minutes prior to perfusion.
Monitor depth of anesthesia using toe pinch reflection.
Achieve deep isoflurane anesthesia, ensuring it takes 5–10 minutes.
Lay the mouse on its back and pin down its four limbs.
Use forceps and dissecting scissors to open the skin and expose the chest cavity.
Cut open the diaphragm carefully without piercing the heart.
Grab at the base of the sternum, cut through the ribcage, and lift it to expose the heart.
Insert the perfusion needle in the apex of the left ventricle.
Cut open the right atrium with fine scissors.
Perfuse the mouse with 1× PBS at room temperature (20°C–23°C) for 5 minutes at a flow rate of 3 mL/min.
Flush the mouse with 4% PFA in PBS for 15 minutes at the same flow rate.
Evaluate success of perfusion by checking whether liver and muscles became pale and hardened.
Remove the mouse’s head, tail, fur from the back and extremities, and internal intestinal organs after successful perfusion.
Place the remaining body into a 50 mL Falcon tube with 4% PFA in PBS for overnight immersion postfixation at 4°C.
Alternatively, dissect out the spinal cord immediately after successful perfusion and place it in a 10 mL Falcon tube with 4% PFA in PBS for overnight immersion postfixation at 4°C.
Transfer the body/spinal cord into PBS with 0.02% sodium azide for storage.
Check after laminectomy if the arteria spinalis anterior is free of blood residue to ensure adequate perfusion.
Dispose PBS 0.02% sodium azide.
Wash the mouse carcass two times with PBS.
Pin the carcass with its paws ventral side up on a Sylgard layer of a dissecting chamber filled with PBS.
Remove all organs, muscles and connective tissue using Dumont 2SP Forceps and Spring Scissors – angled to side by Fine scientific tools GmbH.
Perform a ventral rostral-to-caudal laminectomy to gain access to the spinal cord.
Dissect out the entire spinal cord in a rostral-to-caudal direction.
Pin the dissected spinal cord into a Sylgard chamber using forceps and scissors.
Free the spinal cord from the Dura mater carefully.
Pull all ventral roots towards the rostral direction to reveal their point of origin.
Identify L5 ventral root as a landmark for spinal segment identification.
Count ventral roots starting from L5 to locate the desired segment.
Isolate the spinal segment of interest by cutting right underneath the targeted and next rostral ventral roots with a scalpel.
Mix 5 g of Agar with a total volume of 100 mL 1× PBS in a 250 mL beaker.
Heat the solution in the beaker at 34°C and stir at 400 rpm for 10 min to dissolve Agar completely in 1× PBS.
Pour 8 ml hot Agar (190°C) into disposable weighing pans.
Wait until the Agar stops fuming.
Carefully place the spinal cord segment into the warm Agar (80°C) using forceps.
Trim the solidified Agar block accordingly to the size of the spinal segment.
Cover the Agar block containing the spinal segment in 1× PBS to avoid drying out the tissue.
Glue the Agar block containing the spinal segment in a rostral-vertical orientation onto the platform of the vibratome with Super Glue and wait at least one minute.
Transfer the platform into the cutting chamber of the vibratome filled with 1× PBS.
Cut the segment into 75 μm thick slices with a speed of 7 and frequency 7.
Collect each free floating spinal section directly with a brush and transfer it into 1× PBS in a modified 12-well plate filled with 5 mm Sylgard blackened with graphite powder.
Place one Netwell insert in the well to facilitate handling of the sections during immunohistochemistry.
Avoid adding more than six spinal cord sections into one Netwell insert.
Check intact gross morphology of the spinal cord sections by eye or with a magnification glass before proceeding to the next step.
Incubate sections in blocking buffer (5% normal donkey serum and 0.3% Triton X-100 in 1× PBS) for 90 minutes at room temperature.
Prepare primary antibody combinations according to the antibody list with blocking buffer.
Incubate spinal cord sections in primary antibodies overnight (12–14 h) at 50 rpm on an orbital shaker at room temperature.
Wash sections with 1× PBS for 6 × 10 min the next day.
Prepare secondary antibody solutions for the corresponding primary antibodies.
Incubate sections with secondary antibodies for 3 h at room temperature to visualize primary antibodies.
Apply first the donkey anti-goat Alexa-488 secondary antibody.
Wash the sections 3 × 10 min with PBS.
Apply the Abberior antibody made in goat.
Wash sections with PBS for 3 × 10 min.
Create a hydrophobic barrier on the glass slide with a PAP pen liquid blocker around the slide perimeter.
Mount spinal sections on glass slides with Glycerol/PBS (7:3) mounting medium using a fine brush.
Carefully take out a single section from the PBS solution within the Netwell insert by lifting it up with the brush.
Put the section within the hydrophobic barrier by slowly rolling the brush against the glass slide.
Use a small piece of tissue to remove remaining PBS on the glass slide to avoid sliding of the sections.
Repeat this process for all sections from the same well and place them next to each other.
Recommendation: Do not mount more than six sections per slide, with three sections in the upper row and three sections in the lower row.
Put a drop of Glycerol/PBS (∼60 μL) carefully in the center of the glass slide.
Put cover glass on the slides, push off bubbles and remove extra mounting medium.
Seal the cover glass and slide with nail polish.
Store them at 4°C.
Sections can be stored for several months. Do not start imaging before nail polish is completely hardened (>1 h).
Use highly photostable secondary antibodies for detailed scanning of small structures with STED microscopy.
Scan spinal cord sections with a 10× objective to check gross morphology and relative position within the spinal cord.
Ensure an intact transverse spinal cord section is used for optimal results.
Use an image stack to ∼50 μm of the 75 μm thick transverse spinal section.
Avoid the edges of the section (top and bottom).
Adjust laser intensity appropriately for each channel to improve signal-to-noise ratio.
Scan the 50 μm stack at 0.4 μm z-steps with a resolution of 1024 × 1024 pixels, frequency of 100 Hz, and line average of 4.
Use bidirectional scan for faster imaging acquisition.
Ensure proper intensity of the signal throughout the stack and overall image quality.
Repeat the procedure for two more sections from the same segment for a total of three sections per animal.
Save data file and proceed to image analysis.
Scan vibratome sections with STED microscopy stained with appropriate photostable secondary antibodies suitable for STED.
Locate ChAT+ motor neurons in the ventral horn with a 60× oil objective using confocal mode.
Zoom into a selected proprioceptive synapse of interest with the 60× oil objective and visualize it in confocal mode.
Set a z-Stack for the synapse of interest with the confocal laser.
Adjust laser intensity appropriately to improve signal-to-noise ratio for each channel.
Sequentially scan the synapse in confocal mode for the ChAT+ motor neuron and VGluT1+ proprioceptive synapse.
Scan the intrasynaptic protein Munc13-1 in STED mode.
For STED, use a pixel size of 20 nm, a dwell time of 6 μs, and a line accumulation of 3.
Repeat for ten synapses per animals.
Use LAS X free software from Leica for image analysis of confocal images of premotor synapses onto motor neurons.
Alternatively, use other suitable software such as Fiji-ImageJ or Zeiss ZEN for image analysis.
Count all proprioceptive synapses on the cell body of the motor neuron to avoid biased analysis.
Ensure that only motor neurons with their entire cell bodies scanned in a z-stack are included in the analysis.
Analyze synaptic density on proximal dendrites, as most proprioceptive synapses (95%) are located there.
Go through the z-stack and mark motor neurons whose entire cell body is included in this scan.
Digitally zoom onto one motor neuron cell body.

Slowly go through the z-stack marking every single VGluT1+ proprioceptive synapse over the entire surface of the motor neuron soma using a manual multiple point counter tool such as LAS X or Fiji-ImageJ.
Go back and forward through the z-stack of the entire cell body to ensure no omission or double counting of synapses.
Repeat this procedure for at least 5 motor neurons in one z-stack, and a total of 15 motor neurons per animal.
Proceed with the quantification of synaptic density on dendrites.
Count the number of VGluT1+ synapses over the entire surface of the primary dendrite up to a distance of 100 μm from the soma.
Follow ChAT+ dendrites originating from the motor neuron soma throughout the z-stack.
Divide the length of the dendrite into 50 μm long areas.
Repeat this for at least ten dendrites per z-Stack.
For a total of a minimum of 30 dendrites per animal.
Perform the procedure on at least three animals per genotype.
Count only synapses which are in direct contact with a ChAT signal.
Exclude synapses which are close to motor neurons but not in apposition with dendrites.
